entry.evidence: limited studies on the vertical water structure, in particular on the mixed layer have been accomplished in this region.

steps.action: The authors pose the question of how the vertical water structure and the mixed layer depth vary by season and by area on the Mazandaran shelf, and note that earlier Caspian MLDs were picked visually.
steps.quote: the seasonal and spatial characteristics of the water column are analyzed and the MLD is quantified in the study region.

steps.action: They took CTD profiles on four cross-shelf transects (Amirabad, Babolsar, Noshahr, Ramsar) in spring 2011/2012, summer 2012 and fall 2012, at stations 5 to 180 m deep (83 stations), then removed outliers and duplicates.
steps.quote: Data collections were carried out using an IdronautOcean Seven 316 CTD, equipped with conductivity, temperature and pressure sensors.

steps.action: They interpolated the profiles to 0.5 m and to 1 m bins, found no significant difference between the two, and kept the 1 m bins.
steps.quote: Since no significant differences were observed between these two bins

steps.action: They obtained 3-h air temperature, 3-h wind speed and daily precipitation for the four areas from IRIMO synoptic stations.
steps.quote: is obtained from synoptic stations of IRIMO (Iran Meteorological Organization).

steps.action: They computed conservative temperature, absolute salinity and potential density with TEOS-10 and the Gibbs Seawater toolbox, corrected for Caspian ionic composition after Pawlowicz and Feistel (2012), with a scale factor of 1.228 derived from Millero et al. (2008).
steps.quote: the scale factor for calculating SA in Eq. (2) is determined as 1.228.

steps.action: They designed the MLD estimation: threshold (TM) and gradient (GM) methods on Θ and σθ, four threshold or gradient values each, a 1 m reference depth, visual MLDs as the reference, and four agreement metrics (R2, MAE, RMSE, RAE) plus 1:1 scatter plots.
steps.quote: Two different methods, TM and GM, are used to calculate the MLD based on Θ and σθ profiles with four different THs

steps.action: From the at least 53 stratified profiles, they defined three mixed-layer patterns (classical, inclined, stepwise) by the gradients inside the mixed layer.
steps.quote: Three different patterns, namely classical, stepwise and inclined patterns can be distinguished for the surface density and temperature mixed layer profiles.

steps.action: They counted pattern frequencies by season (Fig. 3): inclined dominates spring, stepwise dominates summer, classical dominates fall.
steps.quote: the classical pattern is extremely frequent in fall for both Θ and σθ

steps.action: They described seasonal air temperature trends (Noshahr taken as representative) and histograms of air temperature, wind and precipitation for each area and season (Fig. 4).
steps.quote: Tair increases sharply during the spring and continues to increase till midsummer with a gentler slope, then begins to decrease.

steps.action: They compared mean atmospheric conditions over the 24 h, 3 days and 7 days before sampling with the seasonal distributions, and set aside short-term forcing as the driver of the profile structures.
steps.quote: the characteristics of the vertical structures cannot necessarily be interpreted based on the shorter than seasonal time-scale conditions.

steps.action: They attributed the patterns to seasonal forcing: spring warming gives inclined layers, fall cooling convection with wind gives classical layers (outweighing high fall precipitation), and mixed forcing in summer gives stepwise layers (Fig. 4f schematic).
steps.quote: The steep increasing trend of Tair in spring, leads to a strong stratification of the surface water

steps.action: Using the transient thermocline and transient mixed layer concepts of Tabata et al. (1965), they reasoned qualitatively which profile shape follows from each combination of heating, precipitation, wind and heat loss in summer.
steps.quote: If the entire transient mixed layer vanishes, we are witnessing a classical mixed layer pattern.

steps.action: They computed MLDs with TM and GM at all threshold and gradient values, illustrated on Ramsar spring 2012 profiles (Fig. 5).
steps.quote: MLD estimated by TM is shown in Fig. 5a, b.

steps.action: They compared computed MLDs with visual MLDs in 1:1 plots (Figs. 6, 7) and metrics (Tables 3, 4). Small thresholds underestimate the MLD; TM at 1 °C (Θ) and 0.5 kg m−3 (σθ) agree best, and TM beats GM.
steps.quote: the best agreement between the mathematical and visual techniques

steps.action: They kept TM on σθ with a 0.5 kg m−3 threshold for the final MLDs, choosing density because it governs water-column stability.
steps.quote: is the most appropriate method to determine the final MLDs.

steps.action: They estimated seasonal MLDs and mixed-layer Θ, SA and σθ (Fig. 8, Table 5): fall 39 ± 5 m, spring 9 ± 3.3 m, summer 21 ± 5.7 m, with seasonal separation in the Θ-SA diagram.
steps.quote: the MLD is maximum in the fall ranges between 30 and 50 m, with the mean and standard deviation of 39 m and 5 m

steps.action: They explained the summer deepening by evaporation-driven salinity increase and convection plus slightly stronger wind, and the high fall salinity by deep convection bringing up salty water.
steps.quote: The main reason for this increase, despite the maximum surface temperature, is the high rate of evaporation in this season.

steps.action: Within each season, they compared vertical sections and mixed-layer properties across areas (Figs. 9, 10; Tables 5, 6), relating differences to shelf slope, sampling date and local weather.
steps.quote: spatial comparisons between different areas are considered separately in each season.

steps.action: They listed untested candidate drivers of the spatial differences (short-term weather, bathymetry, river input, groundwater seepage) and deferred testing to future data.
steps.quote: These variations cannot be explained based on the seasonal atmospheric factors, since many other parameters may be involved

steps.action: They compared their results with earlier Caspian studies (Zaker et al. 2007, Jamshidi and Abu Bakar 2012, Ghaffari et al. 2010) and South China Sea classifications (Tai et al. 2017, Qiu et al. 2019), finding consistency or explained differences.
steps.quote: is completely consistent with what was found by Zaker et al. (2007) in the same season.

steps.action: They kept the seasonal MLD claim (deepest in fall, shallowest in spring), the seasonal attribution of the patterns, and the finding that seasonal variability exceeds spatial variability.
steps.quote: regardless of the region, the MLDs are the deepest during the fall with values between 30 m and 50 m

Rivals are MLD methods and thresholds; for causes, short-term versus seasonal forcing and precipitation versus convection, informally

end.claim: On the SE Caspian shelf the mixed layer is deepest in fall (30-50 m, mean 39 ± 5 m) and shallowest in spring (mean 9 ± 3.3 m), estimated with a threshold method on density profiles (0.5 kg m−3).

decisive_move.sentence: Estimating the MLD at every stratified station with the threshold method chosen against visual MLDs produced the seasonal MLD values on which the headline claim rests.

gates.evidence: Action: the CTD campaigns of 2011-2012 were not directed by a stated hypothesis (p. 4). Claim: the method choice faced a failable test against visual MLDs (Tables 3, 4, p. 7, 10, 11), but the causal attributions (p. 7, 9) were argued from co-occurring atmospheric trends, not tested. Registration: the threshold sets were taken from the literature (p. 4), but nothing is stated as fixed before the data were seen.

imports.item: Pearson coefficient (Pearson 1896) as an agreement metric between computed and visual MLDs
Error metrics MAE, RMSE and relative absolute error (RAE)

novelty_claims.quote: the threshold (TM) and gradient (GM) methods are employed in order to calculate the MLD in the region of study, for the first time.
which is the major contribution of this work
the classification of the mixed layer patterns and their possible links to the atmospheric parameters

limits: Sub-claims at other statuses: (a) the choice of TM on σθ at 0.5 kg m−3 (and Θ at 1 °C) is capability_characterized, but only against the authors' own visual MLDs. The paper criticises earlier visual picking (p. 3) yet uses visual picks as its reference, and reports no inter-observer or blind check of them. (b) The seasonal attribution of the patterns (spring warming, fall convection, summer combined forcing) is best_explanation at most; it rests on co-occurring trends and a qualitative schematic (Fig. 4f) with no flux or model calculation. (c) The spatial differences carry no conclusion; their drivers are only listed (p. 11). Internal inconsistencies, noted from the text: the Methods give σθ gradient values 0.01, 0.05, 0.2, 0.5 kg m−4 (p. 4), but Table 4 and the conclusions use 0.05, 0.15, 0.2, 0.5 (p. 11, 12). The text calls GR 0.2 the best for σθ although Table 4 shows lower MAE, RMSE and RAE for 0.15. The spring MLD range is 3-17 m on p. 9 but 3-19 m on p. 15. Noshahr spring sampling (24 May) is called 'the middle of the summer' (p. 10). Equations 3 and 7 are missing from the typeset version (p. 4). Each season was sampled once per transect, and AmirAbad was not sampled in spring, so seasonal repetition is thin; inference: natures_repetition fits only loosely (no regularity is fitted). The data cannot be shared (p. 15), so no reproduction is possible. No review file was supplied. Coding notes: the XML text holds only the abstract and captions, so body locators are printed pages. The comparisons with earlier studies are coded as replication performed_here: the comparison is made here, but the replicating data are other groups'.

disagreements.quote: in the previous studies the MLD was estimated visually and no mathematical methods have been employed.

disagreements.target: Jamshidi and Abu Bakar (2012), salinity off Anzali
disagreements.support: They explain higher salinity here by the Anzali lagoon outflow, by absolute versus practical salinity, and by a larger salinity coefficient.
disagreements.quote: Salinity values in the study regions are higher than the salinity in Anzali due to the lagoon

disagreements.target: Peeters et al. (2000) salinity coefficient for Caspian water
disagreements.support: They use the Pawlowicz and Feistel (2012) coefficient and note it gives larger salinities; no test between the two is reported.
disagreements.quote: the salinity coefficient proposed by Pawlowicz and Feistel (2012) is larger compared with the one proposed by Peeters et al. (2000).

disagreements.target: Ghaffari et al. (2010), inshore salinity in the western South Caspian
disagreements.support: They attribute the fresher inshore water in the earlier study to inflow from the Anzali lagoon.
disagreements.quote: the inshore waters in the study conducted by Ghaffari et al. (2010) are significantly fresher than those in this study.

disagreements.target: Qiu et al. (2019) four-type classification of vertical structure in the northern South China Sea
disagreements.support: They map Qiu's A-α type to their inclined type and the B type to their classical type, keeping three types.
disagreements.quote: Qiu et al. (2019) divided mixed layer structures in the northern South China Sea into four different types.
